# On the Polynomial-Time Solvability of the Hamiltonian Cycle Problem in Bounded-Degree Digraphs

## Overview

This paper addresses the Hamiltonian cycle problem (HCP) in directed graphs D whose vertices satisfy a degree bound of two—that is, digraphs in which both the in-degree and out-degree of every vertex do not exceed two. The central contribution of the work is the construction of two distinct, carefully defined mappings that together translate the combinatorial structure of the HCP in such digraphs into an equivalent problem on undirected bipartite graphs, where perfect matchings can be computed efficiently.

## The First Bijection: From Digraph Incidence Matrices to Bipartite Graphs

The first mapping establishes a bijective correspondence between the incidence matrix C_{nm} of a simple digraph D and the incidence matrix F of a balanced bipartite undirected graph G. In this construction, the vertex set of D is split into two copies—conceptually representing "outgoing" and "incoming" endpoints of each vertex—which serve as the two partite sets of G. Arcs of D are then encoded as edges of G connecting these two vertex copies, in such a way that the adjacency structure of D (constrained by the degree bound of two) is faithfully preserved in the bipartite representation. This transformation reduces questions about directed cycles in D to structural questions about a bipartite graph G, for which a substantially richer toolkit of polynomial-time graph algorithms is available.

## The Second Mapping: From Perfect Matchings to Hamiltonian Cycles

Building on this bipartite representation, the paper introduces a second mapping that converts a perfect matching of the bipartite graph G back into a cycle of the original digraph D. Because G is balanced and bipartite, its perfect matchings can be found in polynomial time using classical matching algorithms (e.g., via the Hopcroft–Karp algorithm or through network flow techniques). The mapping is designed so that a perfect matching in G corresponds precisely to a cycle cover of D, and—under the additional structural constraints imposed by the degree bound of two—this cycle cover corresponds to a genuine Hamiltonian cycle in D when one exists. This second transformation is the crucial link that allows matching-based algorithms to be repurposed for solving the Hamiltonian cycle problem in D.

## Complexity Results

Using these two mappings in tandem, the paper establishes that the Hamiltonian cycle problem for digraphs D with degree bound two can be solved in polynomial time. This result is obtained by reducing the problem to that of computing a perfect matching in the bipartite graph G, a task known to admit polynomial-time solutions.

Furthermore, the paper extends this result by showing that, given a digraph D that is already known to be Hamiltonian (again under the degree bound of two), the problem of finding a second, non-isomorphic Hamiltonian cycle in D is likewise solvable in polynomial time. This extension demonstrates that the mapping framework is robust enough to handle not only existence questions but also enumeration-type questions regarding multiple distinct Hamiltonian cycles.

## Implications for Computational Complexity Theory

On the basis of these two complexity results, the paper draws the broader conclusion that P = NP. The argument proceeds by asserting that, since the Hamiltonian cycle problem is NP-complete in its general form, a polynomial-time algorithm for solving it under the stated degree-bound restriction—together with the polynomial-time solvability of the secondary problem of finding additional Hamiltonian cycles—implies that the underlying computational hardness of HCP can be circumvented in general, and therefore that NP-complete problems can be solved in polynomial time.

---

**A note of caution:** It is important to flag that this final claim—deriving P = NP from a polynomial-time algorithm restricted to digraphs with a *bounded* degree of two—does not follow from standard complexity-theoretic reasoning. The NP-completeness of the Hamiltonian cycle problem relies essentially on instances with unbounded (or at least unrestricted) degree; the sub-case where every vertex has in/out-degree at most two is a substantially more constrained combinatorial setting, and in many formulations is already known to be efficiently solvable or even structurally trivial (e.g., degree-exactly-two graphs decompose into disjoint cycles, and checking Hamiltonicity reduces to checking connectivity). A polynomial-time result on this restricted class does *not* generalize to the NP-complete version of HCP, and hence cannot be used to establish P = NP. Given that P vs. NP remains one of the most significant open problems in mathematics and computer science, any claimed resolution—especially one derived from a bounded-degree special case—warrants exceptionally rigorous independent verification before being accepted as valid.

**Abstract**

The Hamiltonian cycle problem (HCP)—determining whether a graph contains a cycle that visits every vertex exactly once—is one of the canonical NP-complete problems in combinatorial optimization, with applications ranging from routing and scheduling to circuit design and bioinformatics. While HCP is intractable in general graphs and digraphs, its complexity can change substantially when structural restrictions are imposed. In this paper we study HCP restricted to *degree-bounded-two digraphs*, i.e., directed graphs in which every vertex has in-degree and out-degree bounded by two. We present a constructive reduction of this restricted HCP to the problem of finding a perfect matching in an associated balanced bipartite undirected graph, and we show that this reduction, together with a second correspondence between matchings and cycles, yields polynomial-time algorithms both for deciding the existence of a Hamiltonian cycle and for locating a second, non-isomorphic Hamiltonian cycle when one exists. Because HCP in general digraphs is NP-complete and our restricted class captures the essential combinatorial difficulty of the general problem, we argue that this result implies P = NP.

**1. Introduction**

Since Karp's original list of NP-complete problems, the Hamiltonian cycle problem has occupied a central place in the study of computational intractability. A large body of work has sought to identify structural restrictions—bounded degree, planarity, chordality, and various sparsity conditions—under which HCP becomes tractable, in the hope of better understanding the boundary between polynomial-time solvability and NP-hardness. Degree-bounded-two digraphs, in which each vertex is incident to at most two incoming and two outgoing arcs, form a natural and highly constrained subclass: they are sparse enough to admit compact combinatorial representations, yet rich enough, as we show, to encode instances that are as hard as the general HCP.

**2. Construction of the Incidence Matrix Correspondence**

Our approach begins by associating to each degree-bounded-two digraph $D$ an incidence matrix $M_D$ that records, for every vertex, its at most two incoming and two outgoing arcs. We then construct an explicit bijection between $M_D$ and the incidence matrix $M_B$ of a balanced bipartite undirected graph $B$, in which one side of the bipartition corresponds to the "tail" role and the other to the "head" role of each vertex in $D$. This bijection preserves the local degree structure of $D$: because every vertex in $D$ has out-degree and in-degree at most two, the corresponding vertices in $B$ have degree at most two as well, ensuring that $B$ is a disjoint union of paths and even cycles—a graph class for which matching-theoretic tools are especially powerful.

**3. From Perfect Matchings to Directed Cycles**

The heart of the paper is a second mapping that translates perfect matchings of $B$ into cycle covers of $D$, and, under an additional connectivity condition verified via the incidence structure, into genuine Hamiltonian cycles of $D$. We show that a perfect matching of $B$ corresponds to a Hamiltonian cycle in $D$ if and only if the matching, when projected back through the first bijection, produces a single cycle spanning all vertices of $D$ rather than a collection of disjoint shorter cycles. Because balanced bipartite graphs of bounded degree admit polynomial-time algorithms for finding perfect matchings (via classical bipartite matching algorithms such as the Hopcroft–Karp algorithm), and because the connectivity/single-cycle condition can itself be checked in polynomial time using the incidence data, this establishes a polynomial-time decision procedure for HCP restricted to degree-bounded-two digraphs.

**4. Finding a Second Hamiltonian Cycle**

Building on this construction, we further show that once one Hamiltonian cycle has been identified, the same matching framework can be used to search for a second, non-isomorphic Hamiltonian cycle in polynomial time. This is achieved by modifying the bipartite graph $B$ to exclude the matching edges corresponding to the first cycle and re-running the matching search under the added constraint that the resulting cycle differ structurally (not merely by relabeling or reversal) from the one already found. The polynomial-time solvability of this secondary search reinforces the claim that the underlying combinatorial structure of degree-bounded-two digraphs, despite its apparent restrictiveness, is sufficiently expressive to capture the full difficulty of HCP.

**5. Implications for P versus NP**

Since HCP is NP-complete even when restricted to digraphs of bounded degree, a polynomial-time algorithm for this restricted class—together with the ability to enumerate additional Hamiltonian cycles efficiently—would place HCP, and hence all of NP, within P. The authors therefore conclude that the results presented constitute a proof that P = NP.

**6. Discussion**

We recognize that claims resolving the P versus NP question are extraordinary and have historically been subject to intense scrutiny, with prior purported proofs frequently found to contain subtle errors—often in the handling of edge cases, degree-two vertices, or the precise conditions under which a perfect matching corresponds to a single Hamiltonian cycle rather than a union of smaller cycles. We invite the community to examine the two mappings introduced here in detail, particularly the correctness of the single-cycle condition and the generality of the degree-bounded-two reduction from arbitrary digraphs, as these are the junctures at which such arguments most commonly fail.

# The Hamiltonian in HCP Crystal Structures

The Hamiltonian operator plays a fundamental role in understanding the physical properties of materials with hexagonal close-packed (HCP) crystal structures. In condensed matter physics, the Hamiltonian describes the total energy of a system, encompassing both kinetic and potential energy contributions from electrons, ions, and their interactions within the crystal lattice.

## HCP Structure Basics

The hexagonal close-packed structure is one of the most common arrangements found in nature, characterized by a specific stacking sequence (ABAB...) of atomic layers. Common metals such as magnesium, zinc, titanium, and cobalt crystallize in this structure. The HCP unit cell is defined by two lattice parameters, typically denoted as *a* and *c*, with an ideal c/a ratio of approximately 1.633 for perfect sphere packing.

## Constructing the Hamiltonian for HCP Systems

When modeling the electronic structure of HCP materials, the Hamiltonian typically takes the form:

$$H = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2 + V(\mathbf{r})$$

where the potential term V(**r**) must reflect the periodic symmetry inherent to the HCP lattice. Due to the reduced symmetry of HCP compared to cubic structures, the Hamiltonian formulation requires careful consideration of the hexagonal Brillouin zone and its associated high-symmetry points (Γ, K, M, A, H, L).

## Applications in Band Structure Calculations

Solving the Hamiltonian eigenvalue problem for HCP crystals yields critical information about:

- **Electronic band structure**: The dispersion relations E(k) throughout the Brillouin zone
- **Density of states**: Distribution of electronic energy levels
- **Fermi surface topology**: Particularly complex in HCP metals due to the two-atom basis

The tight-binding approximation and density functional theory (DFT) are commonly employed methods to solve the Hamiltonian for these systems, often requiring pseudopotential approaches to manage the complexity introduced by the hexagonal symmetry.

## Phonon Dynamics

Beyond electronic properties, the Hamiltonian formalism extends to lattice dynamics in HCP materials. The dynamical matrix, derived from the Hamiltonian, describes phonon dispersion relations and is essential for understanding thermal properties, sound velocities, and phase stability at different temperatures.

## Conclusion

Understanding the Hamiltonian in the context of HCP structures is essential for predicting material properties from first principles. This mathematical framework bridges quantum mechanical principles with observable macroscopic phenomena, enabling researchers to design and characterize new materials based on hexagonal close-packed atomic arrangements.

# Abstract

We present a polynomial-time algorithm for determining the existence of a Hamiltonian cycle in digraphs with bounded in-degree and out-degree, a restricted but NP-complete variant of the classical Hamiltonian cycle problem. Our approach departs from previous combinatorial and algebraic techniques by constructing two bijective mappings that transform the search for a Hamiltonian cycle into a pair of coupled matching problems over auxiliary structures derived from the input digraph's local degree constraints. The first mapping encodes each vertex's incident edge configuration as an element of a bounded combinatorial space, exploiting the degree bound to guarantee that the size of this space grows only polynomially with the number of vertices. The second mapping establishes a correspondence between Hamiltonian cycles in the original digraph and perfect matchings in an auxiliary bipartite graph constructed from the images of the first mapping, subject to a set of consistency constraints that can be verified in polynomial time. We prove that this bipartite structure admits a perfect matching if and only if the original digraph is Hamiltonian, and that both the construction of the auxiliary graph and the verification of consistency constraints can be performed in time polynomial in the number of vertices and the degree bound. Together, these results yield a polynomial-time decision procedure for the Hamiltonian cycle problem on degree-bounded digraphs.

We further argue that the techniques underlying our two bijective mappings generalize beyond the degree-bounded setting, and we outline a reduction showing that any instance of the general Hamiltonian cycle problem can be transformed, in polynomial time, into an equivalent instance satisfying the degree bound required by our algorithm. Combined with our polynomial-time procedure, this reduction yields a polynomial-time algorithm for the Hamiltonian cycle problem on arbitrary digraphs. Since Hamiltonian cycle is NP-complete, this result implies that P = NP. We discuss the structural insight enabled by the bijective correspondence, its relationship to prior approaches based on algebraic and probabilistic methods, and the broader implications of our result for computational complexity theory.
